mainEntity.name: How much wax do I need for a candle?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply your container volume by the wax density for your type. For soy wax, one pound fills about 20 oz of container volume. A typical 8 oz candle needs roughly 6.4 oz (0.4 lb) of soy wax.
Fragrance load is the percentage of fragrance oil relative to the total wax weight. Most waxes support 6-10% fragrance load. Soy wax typically maxes at 10-12%, while paraffin can hold 6-10%.

mainEntity.name: What is the density of soy wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Soy wax has a density of approximately 0.9 g/ml (or about 0.86 oz per fluid oz of volume). This means soy wax shrinks slightly when cooling, so containers may need a second pour.

mainEntity.name: How much dye do I use per pound of wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Liquid dye typically uses 3-10 drops per pound of wax, while dye blocks use about 0.1-0.2 oz per pound. Start small and increase until you reach your desired color intensity.

mainEntity.name: Should I fill my candle container all the way?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Fill containers to about 85-90% capacity to leave room for the wick and prevent overflow. This calculator accounts for this fill percentage automatically.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between soy and paraffin wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Soy wax is natural, burns cleaner, and has a lower melting point. Paraffin is petroleum-based, holds more fragrance, and produces brighter colors. Soy is denser so you need less by volume but more by weight.

howItWorks:
How This Calculator Converts Volume Into Wax Weight

Candle wax is sold by weight, but jars and tins are rated by fluid volume. The calculator closes that gap using each wax's specific gravity — how many ounces of solid wax a fluid ounce of melted wax becomes once it cools and sets.

Wax Weight = Container Volume × Fill % × Wax Density

Worked example: Say you're pouring a batch of 12 eight-ounce soy tins at 85% fill. Soy's density factor runs about 0.86 oz per fluid ounce, so each jar takes 8 × 0.85 × 0.86 ≈ 5.85 oz of wax. Across 12 jars that's 70.2 oz, or 4.39 lb, of soy wax to melt. At an 8% fragrance load, you'd add 70.2 × 0.08 ≈ 5.6 oz of fragrance oil to the melt — about 0.47 oz per jar. For color, dye chips run roughly 0.1 oz per pound of wax, so 4.39 lb calls for around 0.44 oz of chips, or somewhere between 18 and 40 drops if you're using liquid dye instead (3-10 drops per pound).

  • Fill percentage accounts for the dome above the wax line and the wick's footprint — pour to 100% of rated capacity and the wax will overflow once it domes on top
  • Wax density is why identical jars need different weights of soy, paraffin, beeswax, or coconut blend — it isn't a rounding detail, it's the conversion factor itself
  • Fragrance oil is a percentage of the wax weight you just calculated, not of the raw container volume — get the weight right first, then take the percentage
  • Dye scales with total wax weight; blocks and chips are measured in fractions of an ounce per pound, liquid dye in drops per pound
faqHTML:
Frequently Asked Questions

How much wax do I need for a candle?

The amount depends on your container volume and wax type. Multiply the container volume by the fill percentage (85%) and the wax density. For soy wax, an 8 oz container needs about 5.8 oz of wax.

What is fragrance load percentage?

Fragrance load is the percentage of fragrance oil relative to wax weight. Most waxes support 6-10%. Going above the recommended maximum can cause sweating, poor burn, or safety issues.

What is the density of soy wax?

Soy wax has a density of approximately 0.86 oz per fluid ounce (0.90 g/ml). It is lighter than paraffin (0.90 oz/fl oz) and beeswax (0.96 oz/fl oz).

How much dye do I use per pound of wax?

For liquid dye, use 3-10 drops per pound. For dye blocks, approximately 0.1-0.2 oz per pound. Start light and increase for deeper colors.

Should I fill my candle container all the way?

No. Fill to 85-90% capacity to leave room for the wick, prevent overflow when the wax melts, and allow for a clean finish. This calculator accounts for fill percentage.

What's the difference between soy and paraffin wax?

Soy wax is plant-based, burns cleaner with less soot, and has a lower melting point. Paraffin is petroleum-based, provides better scent throw, and produces more vibrant colors. Coconut blends offer a middle ground.

howWeCalculate.intro: This tool runs the same weight-from-volume math a chandler does by hand: it converts your container's fluid capacity into a wax weight using the specific gravity of the wax you select, then derives fragrance oil and dye from that weight — never from the raw volume you typed in.
steps: Container volume is multiplied by the fill percentage to get the usable volume — the space wax will actually occupy once you leave headspace for the wick and the dome on top
That usable volume is multiplied by the selected wax's density factor (0.82 to 0.96 oz per fluid ounce depending on type) to convert volume into a wax weight in ounces
Fragrance oil is calculated as a percentage of that wax weight, matching how fragrance load is measured industry-wide — weight of oil per weight of wax, never per volume
Dye amount scales from the same wax weight using standard chip and liquid-dye usage rates, then every figure is multiplied by your candle count for a batch total
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures are starting points based on typical wax densities and common fragrance load ranges. Specific gravity varies by supplier and wax blend, and fragrance oils carry their own usage caps under IFRA guidelines — weigh a test pour on a kitchen scale and check your fragrance oil's data sheet before scaling up to a full batch.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this calculator any time you're moving between container sizes, wax types, or batch sizes and need the actual ounces, not a rough guess scribbled on the back of a recipe card.
scenarios: Scaling a tested recipe from a few sample jars up to a full production run, where a half-ounce error per candle adds up fast across dozens of pours
Switching a recipe between wax types — paraffin to soy, for instance — since the density difference means the same jar needs a different weight of wax
Sizing a bulk wax order before you buy, so you land close to the pounds you'll actually melt instead of running short mid-batch or storing leftover wax for months
Checking whether a repurposed jar or vintage tin will hold the volume your recipe assumes before you commit a full melt pot to it
Working out fragrance oil and dye quantities for a new batch size without re-deriving the ratios from scratch every time

sections.title: What Is the Candle Wax Calculator?
sections.body: Candle recipes are written in weight — ounces or grams of wax, fragrance oil, and dye — but containers are measured in volume. This calculator bridges that gap using each wax's specific gravity, the ratio that tells you how much a given volume of wax weighs once it's melted, poured, and cooled solid. Soy wax runs around 0.86 oz per fluid ounce of volume, paraffin closer to 0.90, beeswax up to 0.96, and coconut-blend waxes down near 0.82. Enter your container's fluid-ounce or milliliter capacity and pick a wax type, and it converts that volume into the pounds and ounces you actually need to melt, along with matching fragrance oil and dye amounts for the batch.

sections.title: Why Density and Fill Percentage Change Your Numbers
sections.body: Two candles poured in identical 8 oz tins won't use identical amounts of wax if the wax type differs. Beeswax is dense and heavy, so a pound of it only fills about 16-17 fl oz of container space, while a pound of soy wax — lighter once set — stretches to roughly 19-20 fl oz. Swapping wax types in the same jar changes your yield-per-pound and cost-per-candle even when nothing else about the recipe changes. Fill percentage matters just as much: pouring to a jar's full rated volume ignores the dome of melted wax above the rim, so most chandlers pour to 85-90% capacity and plan on a second, thinner topping pour once the first layer sets and sinks around the wick.

sections.title: When to Reach for This Before You Melt Wax
sections.body: Use it any time you're scaling a recipe up or down — turning a test batch of three 8 oz jars into a production run of thirty, switching from 4 oz tins to 9 oz tumblers, or figuring out how many jars a 10 lb block of wax will realistically fill once fragrance oil and fill percentage are factored in. It's equally useful before placing a supply order: knowing a 12-jar batch needs about 4.4 lb of wax, 5.6 oz of fragrance oil, and roughly 0.44 oz of dye means you buy close to what you'll use instead of running out mid-pour or sitting on half a bag of wax you won't touch again this year.

howToSteps.title: Measure Your Container's Volume
howToSteps.description: Fill the container with water, pour it into a measuring cup, and enter that fluid-ounce or milliliter figure — this is the number the wax density math runs on, not the jar's marketed size, which is often rounded up.

howToSteps.title: Set Wax Type, Fragrance Load, and Fill Percentage
howToSteps.description: Pick your wax (soy, paraffin, beeswax, or coconut blend), set how many candles you're pouring, and dial in fragrance load — 6-10% is typical, with soy and coconut blends tolerating the higher end — plus a fill percentage around 85%.

howToSteps.title: Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator converts your usable volume into a wax weight using that wax's density, then derives fragrance oil and dye from the resulting weight rather than from the raw volume.

howToSteps.title: Weigh Out Your Melt
howToSteps.description: Use the total wax, fragrance oil, and dye figures to pull your wax, pre-weigh fragrance oil in a separate cup, and shave or drop in dye before you start heating — pour temperature comes after everything else is measured out.

tips: Weigh your empty container, fill it with water, and weigh again — the water weight in grams equals the fluid-ml volume, a more reliable number than trusting a jar's printed capacity.
Soy wax sinks and frosts as it cools, so plan on a second, thinner topping pour about an hour after the first; the total wax figure here already covers both pours combined.
Add fragrance oil once the wax drops to pour temperature, not while it's still at melt temperature — hotter wax causes faster evaporation and a weaker scent throw once the candle cures.
If a fragrance oil's data sheet lists a maximum usage rate below the fragrance load you entered, follow the data sheet — IFRA limits exist for a reason and override general candle-making guidelines.

Liquid dye concentrates fast: start at the low end of 3 drops per pound, let a sample cool to check true color (wax looks darker liquid than solid), and add more before the next pour rather than trying to lighten an already-dyed batch.

faq.question: Why does my soy wax candle need more ounces by weight than the jar's fluid capacity suggests?
faq.answer: It doesn't — weight and volume are different units. An 8 fl oz jar at 85% fill holds about 6.8 fl oz of melted wax, and soy wax's density factor of roughly 0.86 oz per fluid ounce brings that down to around 5.85 oz by weight. The weight figure is smaller than the raw fluid-ounce figure for soy; for denser waxes like beeswax it comes out much closer to equal.

faq.question: Can I use the same fragrance load percentage for every wax type?
faq.answer: No. Soy and coconut-blend waxes generally hold 10-12% fragrance oil before they start sweating oil back out to the surface, straight paraffin tops out closer to 6-10%, and beeswax — dense and naturally aromatic on its own — is usually kept near 6% so added fragrance doesn't fight the wax's own scent or destabilize the pour.

faq.question: How much fragrance oil is too much for one batch?
faq.answer: Past your wax's safe fragrance load, oil separates out as the candle cures, pools on top, or weeps down the jar's side. For the 12-jar soy example above — 4.39 lb of wax at 8% — that's 5.6 oz of fragrance oil; pushing the same batch to 12% would mean 8.4 oz, right at the edge of what most soy waxes can bind before they start sweating.

faq.question: Do I need to adjust dye amounts when I change container size?
faq.answer: Dye scales with wax weight, not container count, so the dye figure here already updates when you change volume or candle count. What it won't catch is dye-lot variation — pigment blocks and liquid dye differ supplier to supplier, so treat the ounce or drop figure as a starting point and confirm the shade in a cooled test pour.

faq.question: What pour temperature should I use once everything is measured out?
faq.answer: That depends on the wax itself, not on the amounts calculated here: soy is typically poured around 130-135°F, paraffin around 160-185°F depending on the blend, and beeswax often needs 150°F or higher just to stay fluid. Add fragrance oil and dye at those temperatures, stir thoroughly, and let the wax cool a few degrees before the final pour to reduce surface frosting.
